before.title: Clutch Slave Cylinder Hydraulic Failure
before.description: The clutch slave cylinder on both NA and NB Miatas is a known wear item — internal seals deteriorate with age and brake fluid contamination, allowing hydraulic fluid to leak past the piston seal. Because the slave's rubber boot can hold a surprising amount of fluid before any external drip is visible, owners often experience a gradually softening clutch pedal long before they spot a leak. Eventually the pedal goes to the floor and the car cannot be shifted into gear (or out of gear once moving). Both the slave and master cylinder share fluid with the brake reservoir, so a slave leak that goes unnoticed can also affect brake-pedal feel.
before.solution: Confirm the leak by pinching the rubber boot on the slave cylinder — trapped fluid will squirt out. Replace the slave cylinder (~$25-$60 part) and bleed the clutch hydraulic system. Because the master cylinder is the same age, many owners replace both at once (~$60-$120 master) and flush the system with fresh DOT 3 fluid. Use the gravity-bleed or reverse-bleed method — the Miata clutch system is notoriously hard to bleed conventionally because of the slave's high-mounted location. RepairPal lists the shop price for slave replacement at $226-$277.
symptoms: Soft, spongy, or sinking clutch pedal
Pedal stays on the floor or returns slowly
Difficulty engaging gears, especially first and reverse at a stop
Brake fluid reservoir level mysteriously drops
Fluid puddles or wet rubber boot at the slave cylinder on the transmission bellhousing

before.title: Convertible Top Rear Plastic Window Cracking and Zipper Failure (NA)
before.description: Original 1990-1997 NA Miatas were fitted with a vinyl convertible top featuring a zippered, clear plastic rear window. The plastic yellows, crazes, and cracks with UV exposure, and folding the top with the window zipped in causes creases that progress to permanent fractures. Additionally, the zipper teeth (and especially the slider) wear out, leaving owners unable to defrost the rear window or seal the cabin properly. By 15-20 years of age virtually all unreplaced original tops have a failed window. NB Miatas (1999+) moved to a heated glass rear window which eliminated this specific issue, though some NBs were also offered with the vinyl/zipper top.
before.solution: Owners have three options: (1) Replace just the plastic window panel using a Robbins or aftermarket zippered window kit ($150-$250 part) — note Mazda used a non-standard zipper, so one half must be sewn into the original top by an upholstery shop ($150-$300 labor). (2) Replace the entire convertible top with a glass-window unit, eliminating the zipper problem permanently ($600-$900 part, $400-$700 install). (3) For a worn slider only, repair kits and the Mazda OEM slider (P/N NA01-R1-250B, ~$4) can restore function for a few more years. Always unzip the rear window before folding the top to prevent recurrence.
symptoms: Clear plastic rear window yellowed, hazy, cracked, or completely torn
Zipper teeth missing or zipper slider that won't engage both halves
Water leaks into the cabin or trunk from a failed seal
Rear window detached at the zipper and flapping in the wind

before.title: Crank Angle Sensor O-Ring and Valve Cover Gasket Oil Leaks
before.description: Two related oil leaks plague essentially every B6 and BP Miata as it ages. (1) The crank angle sensor (CAS, also called the cam angle sensor) at the rear of the cylinder head uses a small O-ring that hardens with age and seeps oil down the back of the block. Because the leak runs down behind the engine, owners often misdiagnose it as a rear main seal failure. (2) The valve cover gasket and its half-moon end seals are a high-mileage failure point — oil weeps onto the exhaust manifold (causing smoke and burning smell) and into the spark plug tubes (fouling plugs and shorting plug wires). Both leaks are inexpensive to repair if caught before they soak the starter, alternator, or motor mounts.
before.solution: Diagnose by sliding cardboard under the engine and noting where drips land — rear means CAS O-ring, front means front crank seal, sides/top means valve cover. CAS O-ring (Mazda P/N B61P-18-235): remove the two CAS bolts, lift the sensor, replace the O-ring (~$5 part), reinstall and align timing. Valve cover gasket kit (~$30-$60) replacement is a 1-2 hour DIY job; torque to 43-78 in-lbs in the correct sequence and apply RTV at the cam cap half-moons. Inspect the PCV grommet and oil filler cap seal at the same time.
symptoms: Oil drip from the rear of the engine (CAS O-ring) or sides of the valve cover
Burning oil smell after driving
Oil pooled in spark plug wells, causing misfires
Wet, oil-soaked starter motor (CAS leak runs down onto it)
Visible oil residue around the cam sensor housing or valve cover perimeter

before.title: Crankshaft Thrust Bearing Failure (1999-2000 BP-4W 1.8L)
before.description: A well-documented manufacturing defect in 1999-2000 NB1 Miatas: the #4 main cap block support was machined with an excessively deep thrust bearing recess, and the factory installed standard-thickness thrust bearings regardless of clearance. The undersized bearing allows the crankshaft to walk fore-and-aft under clutch pedal load. Over time the crank machines into the block, causing the failure mode owners describe as 'pulsing clutch pedal that progresses to stalling when the pedal is depressed at idle.' Most affected engines show symptoms by 40,000-80,000 miles. If ignored, the result is catastrophic engine failure requiring a replacement short block.
before.solution: Diagnose by measuring crankshaft endplay with a dial indicator at the front pulley while an assistant works the clutch pedal: more than ~0.008 in. of movement indicates a failing thrust bearing. Catching the failure early allows replacement of just the thrust bearings (oversize thrust washers are available in 2.625, 2.75, and 2.875 mm). Once the crankshaft journal or block has been machined by the spinning crank, a full engine rebuild or used-engine swap is required. Many owners also replace the clutch and rear main seal at the same time.
symptoms: Pulsing or vibrating clutch pedal
Engine stalls when clutch is depressed at idle
Knocking or grinding noise when clutch pedal is pushed
Excessive crankshaft endplay measured at the front pulley
Difficulty disengaging the clutch as the condition worsens

before.title: Short-Nose Crankshaft Keyway Wear (1990-1991 B6 1.6L)
before.description: Early 1990-1991 Miatas (VIN 209446 and below) were built with a smaller-diameter crankshaft nose (short-nose crank, or SNC) and a 4-slot crank pulley. The design is intolerant of assembly errors and high accessory belt loads: incorrect key installation, improper pulley bolt torque, or aging can allow the crank pulley to wobble on the keyway. The keyway in the crank nose progressively wears, throwing ignition timing off (the crank trigger lives on the pulley), and ultimately can destroy the crankshaft. The 1992 and later large-nose crank (LNC) eliminated this design defect. Owners of affected cars are urged to verify pulley bolt torque to 116 ft-lbs and inspect for visible wobble at idle.
before.solution: Verify crank pulley bolt torque at every timing belt service — 80-87 ft-lbs for the short-nose crank (1990-early 1991, VIN 209446 or less), NOT the 116-123 ft-lbs spec used on the 1992+ large-nose crank. If keyway wear is caught early, the crank can sometimes be salvaged with a Loctite repair and proper torque. If the keyway is destroyed, the only reliable fix is retrofitting the 1992+ large-nose crankshaft, which requires replacing the crankshaft, pulley bolt, cam sprocket, front main seal, crank pulley, spacer, and oil pump as a matched set. For most owners, sourcing a complete 1992+ short block is more cost-effective than the parts swap alone.
symptoms: Visible wobble at the crankshaft pulley while engine is running
Erratic or jumping ignition timing
Loss of power and rough running
Clicking or knocking noise from the front of the engine
Pulley bolt loosening or backing out

before.title: Structural Rust at Rear Rocker Panels and Front Frame Rails
before.description: Both NA and NB Miatas are notorious for hidden structural rust, most commonly at the rear ends of the rocker panels and (especially on NBs) the front frame rails where they meet the floor pan. Water enters via the wheel-arch pinch welds and clogged convertible-top/trunk drain channels and rots the rockers from the inside out. The damage typically goes unnoticed until paint bubbles or a foot goes through the floor. Cars that have only seen winter weather once or twice are still affected; even garaged cars in humid climates show rocker rust. Because the rocker is a structural box section, rust here compromises chassis rigidity and crash safety.
before.solution: Inspect rockers (inside and out) and frame rails at every oil change. Clear the convertible-top drain tubes annually. Surface rust can be wire-wheeled, treated with a rust converter, and protected with a cavity wax (Fluid Film, Woolwax). Perforated rockers must be cut out and replaced with reproduction sheet metal panels (available from Rosenthal and Treasure Coast Miata) and welded in — body shops typically charge $1,500-$3,500 per side for proper repair. Frame rail rot near the lower control arm mounts is a write-off-risk repair and should be evaluated by a competent shop before purchase.
symptoms: Paint bubbling along the lower rocker panel behind the door
Visible perforation at the rear pinch weld where rocker meets rear wheel arch
Soft or holed floor pans next to the seat
Rust flaking from the front frame rails near the lower control arm mounts
Body flex/creaking from a chassis that has lost rocker integrity

proposal.title: Structural Rust at Rear Rocker Panels and Front Frame Rails
proposal.description: The reviewed Mazda/NHTSA inventory did not establish a universal 1990-2005 structural-rust defect at both rear rockers and front frame rails, the claim that one or two winters can affect any car, or the frozen repair-price ranges. Corrosion severity depends on location, exposure, drainage, prior repair and the exact structure involved, so paint bubbles or surface rust cannot establish hidden structural loss without inspection.
proposal.solution: Have a body or frame specialist perform a structural inspection of the rocker cavities, pinch welds, floor attachment points, front rails, suspension mounting areas and convertible-top drainage paths. Remove trim or use a borescope only where the workshop procedure permits, and distinguish surface corrosion from perforation or load-path damage before planning repair. Do not buy rocker panels, frame-rail sections, rust converter, cavity coating or welding supplies from this page; the affected structure and repair design have not been established.
symptoms: paint bubbling or perforation near a rocker or wheel arch
corrosion or deformation at a frame rail or mounting point
water accumulation associated with blocked or damaged drainage
